warmup.q: A consumer runs with default settings. It polls 500 payments, hands them to a thread pool and polls again at once. Six seconds later the service crashes with 200 payments still queued in the pool. After a restart, what happens to those 200?
options: They are delivered again, because Kafka only commits records your code has processed
They are lost: auto-commit, inside a later poll, already committed offsets that cover them
They are delivered again after the session timeout
Kafka notices that the pool didn't finish and rolls the commit back
warmup.why: With enable.auto.commit=true (the default) the consumer commits its positions every 5 seconds inside poll, and the positions cover everything poll has returned, processed or not. Kafka has no idea what your thread pool did. The first option is the common belief that a commit means processed; it only means "read up to here", and here your code moved the bookmark too early.

sections.h: The consumer pulls records in a loop you write
sections.html:
Lesson 6 made the writing side of the log safe: a retried send can't put a payment in the log twice. This lesson moves to the other end. Every messaging system decides when a reader says "done with this one", and that decides what a crash between the work and those words costs: a lost message, or one processed twice. Which of the two a system risks is its delivery guarantee, at-most-once or at-least-once. Lesson 1's queue takes the decision per message, with an acknowledgement for each. A Kafka consumer takes it with one number per partition, and this lesson works out what follows from that.

First, how records reach the consumer at all. A Kafka broker never pushes records to a consumer. The consumer asks for them.

Why pull? Suppose the broker pushed payments as fast as they arrived, 3,000 a second. Your ledger consumer calls a card-issuer API that takes 120 ms per payment, so it handles about 8 a second. A pushing broker would bury it, and something would have to buffer or drop the rest. A queue broker such as RabbitMQ does push, and caps the flood with a prefetch limit: at most so many unacknowledged messages per consumer. With pull, the consumer takes the next records when it is ready, and a slow consumer just falls behind; lesson 2 of this track called that distance lag. Nothing is lost, because the log keeps the records.

The ask is poll(timeout). It returns up to max.poll.records records (500 by default) from the partitions the consumer reads, in offset order within each partition. If nothing new has arrived, it waits up to timeout and returns an empty batch. Under the hood the client sends fetch requests to each partition's leader; the broker answers as soon as it has at least fetch.min.bytes (1 byte by default) or after fetch.max.wait.ms (500 ms), and the client fetches the next batch while your code works on this one.

Your code wraps poll in a loop: poll, process every record, commit, repeat. The next two sections are about that commit. First, two rules for the loop itself.

One thread owns the consumer. KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe, and the only method another thread may call is wakeup(). It makes the current or next poll throw WakeupException, which is how you stop the loop cleanly:

Java
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(consumer::wakeup)); // the only cross-thread call
try {
    while (true) { var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)); /* process, then commit */ }
} catch (WakeupException e) {
    // asked to stop
} finally {
    consumer.close();   // leaves the group, so its partitions move to another consumer at once
}
Kotlin
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread(consumer::wakeup))     // the only cross-thread call
try {
    while (true) { val records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)) /* process, then commit */ }
} catch (e: WakeupException) {
    // asked to stop
} finally {
    consumer.close()    // leaves the group, so its partitions move to another consumer at once
}

And the loop must come back to poll in time. A background thread sends heartbeats, small "still alive" messages to the broker that manages the group, so a busy consumer still looks alive. But if your code doesn't call poll again within max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes), the client assumes the loop is stuck and leaves the group, and another consumer takes its partitions. 500 records at 120 ms each take 60 seconds, which is fine. At 1 second each they take over 8 minutes, and the consumer is thrown out every round. Lower max.poll.records when each record is slow. Lesson 8 covers groups in depth.

sections.h: Two numbers per partition: the position and the committed offset
sections.html:
Lesson 2 said a reader's state is one number. Inside a consumer there are two per partition, and mixing them up causes most consumer bugs.

The position is the offset of the next record poll will return. It lives in the consumer's memory, and poll moves it forward the moment it returns records, before your code has looked at them. After a poll that returned offsets 0 to 9, the position is 10.

The committed offset is the group's saved bookmark. It lives in Kafka, in the internal topic __consumer_offsets, and it moves only when your code commits. It survives a crash. When a consumer starts, or takes over a partition from another member of its group, it asks for the committed offset and sets its position there.

A commit says "everything before this offset is done". So the value is the offset of the next record to read, the last processed offset plus one, as the KafkaConsumer javadoc insists. Commit the last processed offset itself and every restart processes that record again; commit two ahead and every restart skips one.

Compare that with lesson 1's queue. There each message gets its own acknowledgement, and the broker keeps a state for every message: delivered, acknowledged, or still waiting. A Kafka commit is cumulative: one number covers every record before it. That makes it cheap, a single integer per group and partition however many records you read. It also has a price you'll meet in lesson 9: a record that can't be finished holds back everything behind it. The picture is the one from the Replication track: the broker is a leader with a log, and the consumer is a follower that remembers how far it has applied.

There are two ways to commit. commitSync() with no arguments commits the current positions of all the consumer's partitions, which covers everything poll has returned so far. That's right only if you have processed all of it. commitSync(map) commits exactly the offsets you pass, one per partition. Both wait for the broker's answer; commitAsync doesn't wait, so a failed commit is only reported to a callback.

What if the group has no committed offset yet? A new group, or a partition it has never read. Then auto.offset.reset decides. Its default is latest: start at the end, so the new group sees only records written after it started. For a new ledger service on an existing payments topic, that silently skips every payment already there. Use earliest when the history matters, and none when you'd rather fail than guess.

Because the committed offset is just a number in a topic, you can move it. Stop the group, run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets, start it again, and it rereads from wherever you put it. That's how you replay a day of payments after fixing a bug. The Try-it does exactly that.

sections.h: When you commit decides what a crash costs
sections.html:
The position and the committed offset are almost never equal. Between a poll and its commit, the consumer has records in hand that Kafka still counts as unread. What happens to them if the process dies there depends on one decision: commit before you process, or after.

Commit first, then process. If the process dies halfway through the batch, the commit already covers the whole batch. The next consumer starts after it, and the rest of the batch is never processed. Each record is processed at most once, and some never: at-most-once. It suits a metrics feed where a gap is cheaper than a double count.

Process first, then commit. If the process dies halfway, nothing of this batch is committed. The next consumer starts at the old committed offset and receives the whole batch again, including the records already processed. Each record is processed at least once, and some twice: at-least-once. For payments that is the only acceptable choice. A lost payment is a missing ledger entry nobody notices; a repeated one can be detected, and the next section makes it harmless. Step through both below.

Neither name is Kafka's. They describe any messaging system by when the reader records its progress relative to the work. In lesson 1's terms, a RabbitMQ consumer with automatic acknowledgement is at-most-once: the broker counts a message as delivered once it has sent it, so a crash loses it, and the RabbitMQ docs call that mode unsafe. Acknowledging by hand after the work makes it at-least-once.

Now the default you probably run with. enable.auto.commit is true unless you turn it off: every auto.commit.interval.ms (5 seconds), inside a call to poll and in close, the consumer commits its current positions. Those positions cover what the previous poll returned. In a plain loop that's at-least-once with up to 5 seconds of replay, because by the time you call poll again you have processed the previous batch.

It breaks the moment processing leaves the polling thread. Hand the batch to a thread pool or launch a coroutine per record, call poll again right away, and the next auto-commit covers records your workers haven't touched. A crash then loses them. The javadoc states the condition: auto-commit is at-least-once only if you consume all data returned by each poll before the next call or before closing. For payments, set enable.auto.commit=false and commit yourself, after processing.

What about exactly once? The commit goes to Kafka and the processing goes to your database or another API. No ordering of two writes to two systems makes them one atomic step, so a crash between them always leaves one done and the other not. Kafka transactions (lesson 10) make it atomic when both sides are Kafka topics. When the effect lands in a database, you get the same result from at-least-once plus idempotent processing. People call that result exactly-once. Effectively-once is the more honest name: a record may still be processed twice, but its effect lands once.

try.title: Crash a consumer mid-batch, both ways
steps: Run CrashDemo (command below). It writes pay-00 to pay-09, 10.00 EUR each for acct-1, to partition 0. Consumer 1 polls batches of 5 and dies while applying pay-07; consumer 2, a new consumer in the same group, carries on from the committed offset.
Predict what changes when consumer 1 commits before processing, then run it with -Pargs=before instead.

static final Set<String> appliedKeys = new HashSet<>(); // the ledger's idempotency keys static long balanceCents = 0; // acct-1's balance static long start; // the offset of pay-00 public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean commitFirst = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("before"); video.title: Commit before or after: at most once, at least once

sections.h: Duplicates will come, so make processing idempotent
sections.html:
At-least-once means duplicates are certain, not rare. They come from four places: a crash between processing and commit (the previous section), a rebalance, when the group moves a partition to another consumer before the last batch was committed (lesson 8), a producer that sent a payment again after a TimeoutException (lesson 6), and an operator who rewound the group's offsets. So the consumer must make a second delivery harmless. Processing that gives the same result however often it runs is idempotent.

The tool is an idempotency key: a unique id for each business operation, chosen once when the payment is created (the Idempotency-Key header of the API request, or the payment id) and carried in every event about it. The consumer records the keys it has applied and skips a key it has seen. The Caching track's lesson on idempotency keys put the same idea at an API's front door, in Redis; here the consumer checks it at the back. Two tempting substitutes fail. The Kafka offset isn't a key: a producer's resend is a new record with a new offset. And a hash of the content isn't one either: two genuine payments of 40.00 EUR from the same account look identical.

The check and the effect must commit together, in one database transaction:

-- one transaction per payment
INSERT INTO processed_payments (idempotency_key, account_id, amount_cents)
VALUES (:key, :account, :amount);          -- a unique constraint on idempotency_key
UPDATE balances SET balance_cents = balance_cents + :amount
 WHERE account_id = :account;
COMMIT;
-- if the INSERT violates the constraint (ORA-00001 in Oracle), roll back: already applied

Then commit the offset, after the database commit. Walk through the crashes. A crash before the database commit: nothing happened, and the redelivery applies the payment. A crash between the database commit and the offset commit: the redelivery's INSERT hits the constraint and is skipped. Either way the balance moves once. Kafka's design doc notes that exactly-once into another system needs that system's cooperation; its own suggestion is to store the consumer's offset in the same place as the output, which Go deeper shows. The idempotency key is the other way, and the only one of the two that also catches a producer's resend.

Keep each key at least as long as a duplicate can still arrive: the topic's retention (7 days by default) is a safe floor, because a rewind can replay anything still in the log.

Two notes on the lab's version. It keeps the keys in a ConcurrentHashMap instead of a table, which stands in for the database because the test keeps the same ledger while it replaces the crashed consumer. And it processes a whole batch before one commit, so a crash replays up to max.poll.records records. Smaller batches mean less replay and more commits.

The delivery was correct at-least-once: nothing lost. The ledger was not: pay-05 and pay-06 were processed after the last commit and before the crash, so they came again and were credited twice, 20.00 EUR too much. The idempotency check is the only thing between at-least-once delivery and a wrong balance.

analogy: Think of a night clerk entering cheques from a tray into a ledger, with a shift log on the wall. Taking a handful from the tray is poll: the clerk's own place in the tray moves at once. Writing "done up to cheque 105" in the shift log is the commit. If the clerk faints, the next clerk starts from the shift log, not from wherever the first one had got to. Write the log entry before entering the cheques and some are never entered; write it after and some are entered twice, unless each cheque number is checked against the ledger first. The analogy breaks in one place: the tray never empties. Kafka keeps the cheques, so a later clerk can be told to start again from any number.
world: Your Quarkus payment consumers probably don't call poll themselves: the SmallRye Kafka connector runs the loop, and its default commit strategy, throttled (unless you turn auto-commit on), commits an offset only once every message before it has been acknowledged. That's this lesson's at-least-once rule, done for you, so the idempotency check is still yours. Keep the processed-keys table next to the ledger in Oracle and write both in one transaction. If the consumer starts a Temporal workflow per payment instead, use the idempotency key as the workflow id with a reuse policy that rejects duplicates, and a redelivered payment fails to start a second workflow. And check auto.offset.reset on every new consumer group: the default, latest, skips everything already in the topic.
mistake: Treating a committed offset as "processed". Teams leave enable.auto.commit=true, then move processing to a thread pool or coroutines to go faster. The polling thread keeps polling, auto-commit keeps committing, and a crash or a deploy loses every payment that was handed off but not finished, with no error anywhere. It is easy to miss because it works perfectly until the process dies. The fix: set enable.auto.commit=false, commit only offsets whose records are fully processed (with handed-off work, the lowest unfinished offset per partition), and make processing idempotent so the replay this causes is harmless.

compare.title: An at-least-once payment loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments")); try { while (true) { ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { ledger.apply(Payment.parse(r.value())); // idempotent: a repeat is skipped } if (!records.isEmpty()) consumer.commitSync(); // only after the whole batch } } catch (WakeupException e) { // shutdown requested } finally { consumer.close(); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: consumer.subscribe(listOf("payments")) try { while (true) { val records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)) for (r in records) { ledger.apply(Payment.parse(r.value())) // idempotent: a repeat is skipped } if (!records.isEmpty) consumer.commitSync() // only after the whole batch } } catch (e: WakeupException) { // shutdown requested } finally { consumer.close() }

compare.note: The same loop line for line. Kotlin iterates ConsumerRecords directly because it is a Java Iterable, and reads isEmpty() as the property isEmpty. commitSync() without arguments is correct here only because the loop processed every record poll returned; if it could stop part-way through a batch, it would have to pass explicit offsets instead. Kotlin's use { } would also close the consumer, but the explicit finally keeps the shutdown order visible in both.

drill.prompt: Write, from memory, the body of an at-least-once poll loop for one batch: poll, apply each payment to an idempotent sink, then commit the right offsets per partition with commitSync(map). Then answer: a batch held offsets 40 to 49 of partition 2, you applied all ten, and you commit 49. What happens after a restart?

answer.html: val records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)) for (r in records) sink.apply(Payment.parse(r.value())) // process the whole batch first if (!records.isEmpty) { consumer.commitSync(records.partitions().associateWith { tp -> OffsetAndMetadata(records.records(tp).last().offset() + 1) // next to read: last + 1 }) } // Committing 49 says "49 is the next record to read": after a restart, offset 49 is delivered // again. The idempotent sink skips it, but the commit should have been 50.

alt.html: ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)); for (var r : records) sink.apply(Payment.parse(r.value())); // process the whole batch first if (!records.isEmpty()) { Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> offsets = new HashMap<>(); for (TopicPartition tp : records.partitions()) { List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> rs = records.records(tp); offsets.put(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(rs.get(rs.size() - 1).offset() + 1)); // last + 1 } consumer.commitSync(offsets); } // Committing 49 says "49 is the next record to read": after a restart, offset 49 is delivered // again. The idempotent sink skips it, but the commit should have been 50.

recap: Consumers pull: poll returns up to max.poll.records (500) records from the position onwards. One thread owns the consumer; wakeup() is the only call another thread may make.
The position is in memory and moves when poll returns. The committed offset is saved in __consumer_offsets, moves only on commit, and is where a restarted or new consumer begins.
Commit the next offset to read, last processed plus one. A group with no committed offset starts at auto.offset.reset, which defaults to latest.

Commit after processing for at-least-once, before for at-most-once: the same choice a queue consumer makes with its acknowledgements. Auto-commit is at-least-once only if each batch is finished before the next poll.
At-least-once means duplicates: make processing idempotent with an idempotency key stored in the same transaction as the effect, then commit the offset.
Call poll within max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes), or the consumer leaves the group; lower max.poll.records when records are slow.

explain.prompt: In an incident review someone says: "We commit offsets, so every payment is processed exactly once." Explain what a commit guarantees, what can still go wrong, and how the ledger consumer gets exactly-once results.
explain.answer: A commit only saves a bookmark: the group's committed offset, the next record to read after a restart. It says nothing about what our code did. If we commit before processing, a crash loses the rest of the batch; if we commit after, a crash replays everything since the last commit, so some payments are delivered twice. Auto-commit is worse if we hand records to other threads, because it commits records nobody has finished. Duplicates also come from producer resends and from rewinding offsets. So we commit after processing, which gives at-least-once delivery, and make the processing idempotent: every payment carries an idempotency key, and the ledger inserts the key and updates the balance in one Oracle transaction, with a unique constraint on the key. A redelivered payment hits the constraint and is skipped. Only after the database commit do we commit the offset. That gives exactly-once results in the ledger, even though delivery is at-least-once.

deeper.html:
Store the offset with the effect. Instead of deduplicating by key, some consumers write the offset into the database in the same transaction as the effect (a table of topic, partition and next offset), and never commit to Kafka at all. On start, and whenever the group hands it a partition, the consumer reads that row and calls seek. Then the effect and the bookmark can't disagree, which is exactly-once into that one database. The KafkaConsumer javadoc describes this pattern; it needs a ConsumerRebalanceListener to seek on assignment, which lesson 8 covers. It doesn't remove the need for idempotency keys if producers can resend, because a resend is a new offset.

commitAsync. commitSync blocks the loop for a round trip per batch. A common pattern is commitAsync inside the loop and one commitSync in the finally before close. An async commit that fails is only reported to its callback and is not retried, because a retry could land after a newer commit and move the bookmark backwards; the next successful commit covers it anyway.

Testing. MockConsumer, used in this lesson's lab, implements the whole Consumer interface in memory. addRecord, setMaxPollRecords, schedulePollTask and setPollException let a test script exactly which batches arrive and when wakeup fires, so the loop's commit logic can be tested in milliseconds. Keep one broker test for what a mock can't show, such as a real group handing partitions over after a crash.

The same idea in a textbook. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, sets acknowledgement-based brokers next to log-based ones and makes the follower comparison from section 2: a consumer's offset works like a replica's position in its leader's log, so after a crash it resumes from the last recorded position and may repeat whatever came after it.
